data.intent: Get fully prepared for a fintech job interview next week: research the company, line up stories and technical practice, track the interview stages, and have references and timers ready.

suggestions.title: 7-day prep plan
suggestions.reason: A day-by-day schedule so prep is spread across the week and nothing is left to the last night

content.text: Interview prep plan
Goal: walk in confident on the company, the role, my stories, and the technical basics.
Days 1-2: Research
Re-read the job description and highlight the top 5 requirements
Complete the company research brief
Look up interviewers on LinkedIn
Days 3-4: Stories and technical practice
Write 6-8 STAR stories in the story bank
Work through the technical practice tracker, weakest topics first
Refresh fintech fundamentals: payments flow, KYC/AML, compliance basics
Days 5-6: Mock interviews
Do one timed mock behavioral interview out loud
Do one timed technical mock
Finalize questions to ask the interviewers
Day 7: Final prep
Pick the outfit, test the video link and audio, or plan the route
Skim the research brief and pitch once, then stop and rest

suggestions.title: Company research brief
suggestions.reason: One place to capture what the company does, how it makes money, and where it sits in the market

content.text: Company research brief
What they do
One-sentence product summary, who the customers are (consumers, SMBs, banks), and the core problem they solve.
Business model
Revenue sources: interchange, subscriptions, interest, SaaS fees, take rate?
Funding stage, latest round, and key investors
Headcount and growth trend
Competitors and positioning
Top 3 competitors and how this company differs
Incumbent banks or processors they compete against
Regulation and risk
Licenses held, banking partners, and regulators involved. Note any recent compliance news or enforcement actions.
Recent news
Read the last 3 press releases or blog posts
Check recent funding or product launch coverage
Find the CEO's recent talks or interviews
How I fit
Match 3 of my experiences directly to the top requirements in the job description.

content.text: Questions to ask
About the role
What would success look like in the first 90 days?
What is the biggest challenge the team is facing right now?
About the business
How do regulatory requirements shape the product roadmap?
Where do you see the company in 2-3 years, and what is the main growth lever?
About the team and culture
How does the team make decisions and handle disagreement?
What do you enjoy most about working here?
Next steps
What does the rest of the process look like, and when can I expect to hear back?

Add this month's rent charges to the Rent payments table

Check for leases expiring in the next 90 days

Reconcile payments against the bank account

content.text: Japan Family Trip – 14 Days
Four travelers, two weeks, a mix of big-city energy, history and downtime. Keep days light enough for kids and jet lag.

Tokyo – 5 nights (Asakusa, Shibuya, teamLab, day trip to Kamakura or Nikko)
Hakone – 1 night (ryokan with onsen, Lake Ashi, views of Mt. Fuji)
Kyoto – 4 nights (Fushimi Inari, Arashiyama, Gion, Nara day trip)
Osaka – 3 nights (Osaka Castle, Dotonbori, Universal Studios Japan)
Final night near the airport, then fly home
Priorities & ground rules
Max two big activities per day, with a rest block after lunch

Family extras
Snacks and entertainment for long train rides
Small gifts (omiyage) for hosts or new friends

Empty space in luggage for souvenirs

data.title: Project Brief: Migrating the Team Wiki to PlexiiWrite

content.text: Purpose

This brief outlines the plan to move our team wiki into PlexiiWrite. It is meant to align everyone on why we are doing this, what is and is not included, when it will happen, and what could go wrong. It is a first draft and should be edited with the details only the team knows.
Background

Our team wiki currently lives in [current wiki tool]. We have decided to consolidate it in PlexiiWrite because [primary reason for the move, e.g. cost, consolidation, better editing]. Project owner: [owner name]. Executive sponsor: [sponsor name].
Goals
The migration should achieve the following:
Move all content we still use into PlexiiWrite with structure, links and formatting intact.
Make pages easier to find, with a clear top-level organization and consistent naming.
Retire the old wiki cleanly so there is one source of truth, not two.
Keep disruption to day-to-day work low, so people can find what they need throughout the move.
Success will be measured by [success measures, e.g. share of pages migrated, team adoption, time to find a page], reviewed at [review date].
Scope
In scope:
Content audit of the existing wiki to decide what to migrate, archive or delete.
Migration of approved pages, attachments and embedded media.
Setting up the page hierarchy, permissions and templates in PlexiiWrite.
Fixing internal links and any external links that point to the old wiki.
Short guidance for the team on where things now live and how to edit them.
Read-only archiving and eventual shutdown of the old wiki.
Out of scope:
Rewriting or substantially improving content that is being migrated, beyond fixes needed to make pages work.
Integrations with other tools, unless listed here: [any required integrations].
Migrating content owned by teams outside [participating teams].
Timeline
Dates are placeholders to be confirmed with the owner.
Audit and content inventory: [start date] to [end date]
Structure, permissions and templates set up in PlexiiWrite: [dates]
Pilot migration of a small section, with feedback: [dates]
Full migration: [dates]
Content freeze on the old wiki: [date]
Old wiki set to read-only: [date]
Old wiki shut down: [date]
Risks and Mitigations
Content does not convert cleanly, leaving broken formatting, tables or attachments. Mitigation: run a pilot first, document known problems, and assign page owners to check their own sections.

Broken links, both inside the wiki and from other tools, emails or documents that point to old pages. Mitigation: keep the old wiki read-only for a set period and maintain a list of high-traffic pages to redirect or re-link.
Edits made in the old wiki during migration are lost. Mitigation: announce a clear content freeze date and stick to it.
Outdated content gets migrated and clutters the new space. Mitigation: use the audit to archive or delete before moving anything.

Low adoption, with people continuing to use the old wiki or scattering notes elsewhere. Mitigation: communicate early, name the new home clearly, and have [owner name] check in with the team after launch.
Permissions are set incorrectly, exposing sensitive pages or blocking access. Mitigation: review access for restricted sections before go-live.
The timeline slips because the migration competes with regular work. Mitigation: agree on time commitments from contributors up front: [expected time commitment].
Roles
Project owner: [owner name], responsible for the plan and decisions.
Migration lead: [name], responsible for execution and technical issues.
Section owners: [names], responsible for reviewing their content before and after migration.
Next Steps
Confirm the owner, sponsor and participating teams.
Fill in the dates above and share the brief for comment.
Begin the content audit.

content.text: Welcome

Welcome to the support team. This guide covers what you will do in your first week, the tools you will use, and how we handle escalations. It is meant to be read once at the start and then used as a reference. Nobody expects you to remember everything on day one. Your job this week is to learn how we work, ask plenty of questions, and get comfortable handling real conversations with a safety net underneath you.
Your onboarding buddy is [buddy name], and your manager is [manager name]. If you are unsure about anything, ask your buddy first. If they are unavailable, post in [team chat channel].
Your First Week
The plan below is a suggested shape for the week. Your manager will confirm the exact schedule and any changes.
Day one: get set up

Today is about access and orientation. You will meet your manager and buddy, confirm that your accounts work, and read through this guide. Make sure you can log in to every tool listed in the next section before the day ends. If anything is missing, tell [IT or access contact] right away rather than waiting.

You will also get an overview of what we do, who our customers are, and what a good support interaction looks like here. Ask for a short walkthrough of our product from the customer's point of view if you have not used it yet.
Days two and three: shadow and learn

Spend these days watching experienced agents handle live conversations, and read a sample of past tickets that were resolved well. Pay attention to tone, how agents ask clarifying questions, and how they decide when to look something up versus answer from memory. Read our knowledge base articles for the most common issue types, which your buddy will point you to.
Take notes on anything confusing. A running list of questions is one of the most useful things a new agent can keep.
Day four: handle tickets with review

You will start answering real tickets, with your buddy reviewing replies before they are sent where possible. Start with simpler, lower-risk issue types. Expect feedback, and treat it as part of the training rather than a verdict on your work.
Day five: work more independently and check in

You will take on a larger share of the queue and send more replies without pre-review. At the end of the day, you and your manager will hold a check-in to talk about what went well, where you feel unsure, and what the plan is for week two. Come with your list of questions and any suggestions for improving this guide.
Tools You Will Use
You will work in a small set of tools every day. The list below names each category, and the placeholders should be replaced with our actual tools.
The help desk, [help desk tool], is where tickets arrive, are assigned, and are answered. Learn how to filter your queue, apply tags, set statuses, and add internal notes.
The knowledge base, [knowledge base tool], is where you find answers and where you will eventually help improve articles when you spot gaps or errors.
Team chat, [chat tool], is for quick questions, urgent flags, and staying in touch with the team. Use [channel name] for questions and [channel name] for urgent issues.
The admin or account lookup tool, [admin tool], lets you view customer accounts. Access levels vary, so ask your manager what you can view and change.
The issue tracker, [issue tracker], is where bugs and engineering requests are logged and followed.
Reporting and quality tools, [tool name], show how your work is measured. Your manager will explain which metrics matter and how they are used.

Handle customer data with care. Only open accounts you need to open to solve a specific ticket, and never share customer information outside approved channels. If you are unsure whether something is safe to share, ask before you send.
Working a Ticket Well

A few habits will serve you throughout your time here. Read the whole conversation history before replying, so the customer never has to repeat themselves. Confirm you understand the problem in your own words when it is not obvious. Give a clear next step in every reply, even when the answer is that we are still investigating. Be honest about what you do not know, and never promise something you cannot deliver, such as a fix date or a refund, unless policy clearly allows it.
Our response and resolution targets are [response time targets]. Your manager will explain how they apply to different ticket types.
How We Handle Escalations

An escalation means passing a ticket to someone with more expertise, authority, or access than you have. Escalating is a normal and expected part of the job, and it is never a sign of failure. The mistake to avoid is holding on to a ticket too long when the customer needs something you cannot give them.
When to escalate
Consider escalating when any of these apply:
The issue looks like a bug or outage rather than a usage question.
The customer needs a decision outside your authority, such as an exception to policy, a refund above your limit of [refund limit], or a contract matter.
The issue involves security, privacy, legal concerns, or possible data loss.
The customer is at risk of leaving, or has asked for a manager.
You have tried the documented steps and still cannot resolve it, or you are unsure what to do next.
The ticket is approaching or has passed its target time with no clear path to resolution.
If you are not sure whether something warrants escalation, ask your buddy or post in [channel name]. Asking early is always better than asking late.
Severity levels
We sort escalations by impact so the right people respond at the right speed. Replace the descriptions and times below with our actual definitions.
Critical, [definition], with a response target of [time] and escalation to [role or on-call contact].
High, [definition], with a response target of [time] and escalation to [role or team].
Normal, [definition], with a response target of [time] and escalation to [role or team].
How to escalate
Follow the route set out in [escalation process document or link]. In general, the steps are:
Tell the customer what is happening. Let them know you are bringing in a colleague or team, and set a realistic expectation for when they will hear back, based on the targets above.
Write a clear handoff note in the ticket. The person picking it up should not need to ask you basic questions.
Assign or route the ticket to [team or queue name], and flag it in [chat channel] if it is high or critical severity.
Stay involved. Keep the ticket on your radar until it is resolved, and follow up if the customer has not heard back within the expected time.
What a good handoff note includes
A short summary of the problem and its impact on the customer.
The customer's account details or identifiers, where relevant.
Exact steps to reproduce the problem, if it is technical, along with any error messages or screenshots.
What you have already tried and what the result was.
What the customer has been told so far, including any commitments.
What you need from the person you are escalating to, such as a fix, a decision, or advice.
After the escalation

Once the issue is resolved, close the loop with the customer personally if you can. Then ask what you could learn from the case. If it exposed a gap in our documentation or a recurring problem, add a note in [location] or tell your manager. This feedback is how our knowledge base and processes get better.
Who to Ask
For day-to-day questions, ask [buddy name] or post in [channel name].
For schedule, performance, or wellbeing matters, talk to [manager name].
For access and equipment issues, contact [IT or access contact].
For urgent customer-impacting issues outside normal hours, follow [on-call process].
First Week Checklist
I can log in to every tool I need.
I have met my buddy and manager.
I have read the knowledge base articles for our most common issue types.
I have shadowed at least [number] live conversations.
I have answered tickets and received feedback.
I understand when and how to escalate, and where the escalation process is documented.
I know who to ask when I am stuck.
I have a check-in booked with my manager for the end of the week.
A Final Note

You will make mistakes in your first weeks, and so has everyone on this team. What matters is that you ask questions, learn from feedback, and treat each customer as a person with a problem they want solved. We are glad you are here.

slides.title: How to Write a Good Bug Report
slides.notes: Welcome everyone. Today is about one small skill that saves the whole team time: writing a bug report that someone else can act on without chasing you for details. This will take [session length] and end with a short exercise.

slides.title: Why a good report matters
bullets: A clear report gets fixed faster
A vague report starts a back-and-forth
Developers can only fix what they can reproduce
Your report is often read weeks later by someone with no context
Good reports also help with triage and prioritization
slides.notes: Frame this as respect for the reader's time. The person picking up your report may not have been in the conversation where you found the problem, so the report has to stand on its own. Ask the room for a time they received a report that said only 'it's broken'.

slides.title: The anatomy of a strong report
bullets: A short, specific title that names the problem
Steps to reproduce, numbered and in order
Expected result versus actual result
Environment: device, browser or app version, operating system
Evidence such as screenshots, recordings or logs
Severity and who or what is affected
slides.notes: Walk through each part in order and say why it exists. The title helps people scan a list, the steps let someone reproduce it, and the expected versus actual comparison shows what you believe is wrong. Mention that your team's tracker may have a template, and show it here: [name of your bug tracker or template].

slides.title: Weak report, strong report
bullets: Weak title: 'Checkout is broken'
Stronger title: 'Checkout button does nothing after applying a discount code'
Weak steps: 'Try to buy something'
Stronger steps: numbered actions from a known starting point
Weak outcome: 'It doesn't work'
Stronger outcome: what you expected, and what happened instead
slides.notes: Read the weak and strong versions aloud and let the contrast do the work. Point out that the stronger version is not longer for its own sake; it is more specific. If you have a real anonymized example from your own tracker, swap it in here: [example ticket].

slides.title: Habits that make reports better
bullets: Reproduce the bug at least once more before filing
Search for duplicates first
Report one problem per ticket
Stick to facts and keep blame and opinion out
Note how often it happens: every time, sometimes, once
Attach evidence at the moment you see it
slides.notes: These are small habits, not extra paperwork. Reproducing it a second time often reveals the missing step or condition. Keeping one problem per ticket means each can be assigned, fixed and closed independently.

slides.title: Your turn
bullets: Take the vague report on screen
Rewrite the title, steps and expected versus actual result
Add the environment details you would need
Share with a partner and compare
Checklist: could a stranger reproduce this?
slides.notes: Give the group [exercise time] to rewrite the sample report: [sample vague report]. Close by repeating the one test that matters: could someone with no context reproduce this from the ticket alone? Then point people to [where to find the template or guidelines].

Subject: Kickoff for the Plexii Pulse launch

Hi team,

Thanks for making time to get Plexii Pulse off the ground. This note sets out what we are aiming for, the rough shape of the timeline, and who owns each piece, so everyone starts from the same page. Please reply with corrections or gaps before [kickoff meeting date].

What we are aiming for

The launch has one main goal: [primary goal, for example the outcome Plexii Pulse should achieve at launch]. To know whether we got there, we will track [success metric 1] and [success metric 2], measured against [target and timeframe].

Beyond that, we want a launch that is calm and well prepared. That means the product is ready when we say it is, customers hear about it from us in a consistent way, and support and sales are ready for the questions that follow.

Timeline

These are the milestones we will work toward. Dates are placeholders until we confirm them together in the kickoff meeting.

MilestoneTarget date

Launch day[launch date]
Post-launch review[date]

Who owns what

Each workstream has a single owner who is accountable for it, even when several people contribute. If you think an area is missing or the split is wrong, tell me and we will adjust it.

Overall project and timeline[owner name]Plan, status updates, risks, go or no-go

Next steps

Thanks again, and I am looking forward to getting this launched with you.

[Your name]
